unit-m31.title: Topic 3 · 3-1 Patterns with Exponents and Powers of 10
unit-m31.source: enVision Math, Topic 3 textbook scan — Lessons 3-1 to 3-7 (Drive)

summary.text: Lesson 3-1 introduces exponents: the base is the number being repeated, the exponent counts how many times, and a power of 10 has exactly as many zeros as its exponent. Multiplying a number by a power of 10 attaches that many zeros.

why.text: Exponents are how big numbers stay readable — 10⁶ is easier to compare than 1,000,000 with the zeros counted by eye. The zeros pattern from this lesson is also the engine behind the decimal place-value work in the rest of the topic.

objectives.text: Write a power of 10 using an exponent, and read one back into a whole number.
Multiply a single digit by a power of 10 using the zeros pattern.
Explain the mistake when exponents are added instead of multiplied.

parentNote.text: First lesson of Topic 3, and the class has jumped books — this is 5th-grade material, which is how her accelerated track works. The classic error to watch for: reading 10⁴ as 10 × 4 = 40. The lesson check and everything after leans on the zeros-equals-exponent pattern.

nextUp.text: Cards first — exponent and base have to be solid words before the pattern makes sense. Then the quiz.

cards.def:
**The small raised number that tells how many times to use the base as a factor.**
• In 10³, the 3 means: multiply three 10s together.
• 10³ = 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000.
cards.hint: The exponent counts copies, it never multiplies itself.

cards.def:
**The number the exponent repeats.**
• In 10³, the base is 10 — it is the number being multiplied.
• The exponent only says how many times.
cards.hint: Base = the big number on the ground floor.

cards.def:
**10 multiplied by itself one or more times: 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000…**
• 10¹ = 10, 10² = 100, 10³ = 1,000.
• Every step up multiplies by another 10.
cards.hint: Each power is one storey higher — ten times higher.

cards.def:
**For a power of 10, the exponent equals the number of zeros in the product.**
• 10⁴ = 10,000 — four zeros.
• This is the pattern that makes exponents fast to read.
cards.hint: Count the zeros; you have read the exponent.

cards.def:
**Write the other factor, then attach as many zeros as the exponent.**
• 7 × 10³ = 7,000.
• The factor does not change — only zeros are attached.
cards.hint: The 7 stays a 7; the 10s only bring zeros.

questions.hint: The exponent counts how many zeros the answer has.
steps: The base is 10 and the exponent is 4.

ex.main: **10,000.** Four 10s multiplied together — and four zeros, matching the exponent.
ex.tip: The trap answer 40 comes from multiplying 10 × 4. The exponent never multiplies.

questions.q: How is 100,000 written as a power of 10?
steps: Count the zeros in 100,000: there are five.
For a power of 10, zeros and exponent match.

ex.main: **10⁵.** Five zeros, exponent 5 — the pattern in both directions.
ex.tip: Writing big round numbers this way is why scientists love exponents.

questions.q: In the expression 10⁶, which number is the base?
questions.hint: The base is the number being repeated.
steps: The base is the number the exponent copies.
So the base is 10, and 6 is the exponent.

ex.main: **10.** The 6 is the exponent — it counts, it is never a factor itself.
ex.tip: 1,000,000 is the VALUE of 10⁶, not its base.

questions.q: A crate holds 4 × 10³ oranges. How many oranges is that?
steps: Write the 4 and attach three zeros: 4,000.

ex.main: **4,000.** The exponent 3 attaches three zeros to the 4.
ex.tip: A quick check: the number of zeros in the product matches the exponent.

questions.q: A city library has 8,000,000 pages across all its books. Which expression equals 8,000,000?
steps: Count the zeros in 8,000,000: six of them.

ex.main: **8 × 10⁶.** Six zeros, exponent 6 — reading the pattern backwards.
ex.tip: Going from the big number back to the exponent is the same pattern in reverse.

questions.q: How many zeros does the product 5 × 10⁴ have?
questions.hint: The 5 brings no zeros of its own.
steps: The product keeps exactly the four zeros the power of 10 brought.

ex.main: **4.** The zeros come from the power of 10; the 5 just sits in front of them.
ex.tip: If the front factor ended in 0 (like 50), the product would gain an extra zero — watch for that case later.

questions.q: A farm ships 3 × 10² melons. If the exponent changed from 2 to 3, what would happen to the number of melons?
opts: It would be 10 times as many
It would be 100 times as many
steps: Raising the exponent by one multiplies by one more 10.

ex.main: **10 times as many.** Each step up in the exponent is one more ×10.
ex.tip: Exponents grow multiplicatively — one step never just adds.

questions.q: A student writes 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 40. What mistake did they make?
opts: They forgot to attach zeros to the 4
They added the 10s instead of multiplying them
questions.hint: Check: what operation actually produces 40 from four 10s?
steps: The student added where the expression says multiply.

ex.main: **They added instead of multiplied.** Four 10s multiplied make 10,000, not 40.
ex.tip: Saying HOW an answer went wrong is a stronger skill than just marking it wrong.

questions.hint: The exponent says how many zeros follow the 6.
steps: Five zeros after the 6 — matching the exponent.

ex.tip: The 650,000 trap slips a digit into the zeros — the front factor never leaks into them.

questions.q: A telescope can see about 90,000 stars on a clear night. Which expression equals 90,000?
steps: 10,000 has four zeros, so it is 10⁴.

ex.tip: 90 × 10⁴ is a trick worth pausing on: it equals 900,000 — the zero inside 90 counts too.
